name: Transistor
tagline: Publish a private or public RSS feed from user-owned audio storage

tiers.name: Starter
tiers.limits: Unlimited podcasts and team members; 50 private subscribers; 20,000 downloads/month
tiers.notes: Annual equivalent calculated from paying for 10 months and receiving 12.

tiers.name: Professional
tiers.limits: Unlimited podcasts/team; 500 private subscribers; 100,000 downloads/month; dynamic ads

tiers.name: Business
tiers.limits: Unlimited podcasts/team; 3,000 private subscribers; 250,000 downloads/month; branding removed

tiers.name: Enterprise
tiers.limits: Starts at custom download, subscriber, support and service limits
tiers.notes: Published as $199+/month; annual equivalent calculated from the 10-month-for-12 offer.

pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual; annual is priced as 10 months for 12
pricing.hiddenCosts: Transcription is sold in separate 5-hour and 20-hour add-ons with no public unit price; sustained download overages require an upgrade or sales discussion.

verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For Transistor, publish a private or public RSS feed from user-owned audio storage. The hard boundary is reliable hosting, multiple shows, analytics, team access, and directory support, plus audio infrastructure, distribution, and production polish.
coreLoopDIY: Import spoken-word audio, perform practical cleanup, assemble an episode with show notes, and publish a private or public RSS feed from user-owned audio storage.
whatYouLose: reliable hosting, multiple shows, analytics, team access, and directory support
moatNotes: audio infrastructure, distribution, and production polish
ongoingBurden: codec support, loudness standards, transcription, storage, feeds, analytics, and deliverability to directories
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Transistor because creators pay to remove fragile audio plumbing and publishing chores from a release schedule. The recurring cost buys codec support, loudness standards, transcription, storage, feeds, analytics, and deliverability to directories, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Audacity
priorArt.desc: Long-running open-source multitrack audio editor and useful implementation prior art.

alternatives.name: Castopod
alternatives.desc: Podcast hosting on your server, complete with feeds, analytics and comments; you inherit the server.

alternatives.name: Podlove Podcast Publisher
alternatives.desc: A serious WordPress podcast publisher, provided WordPress is already a life choice.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Starter plan and a single-creator production tool DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for Transistor in an empty repository.
Use Python 3.12, FastAPI, ffmpeg, SQLite, and an HTMX interface; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: import spoken-word audio, perform practical cleanup, assemble an episode with show notes, and publish a private or public RSS feed from user-owned audio storage.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Create an upload queue and preserve originals in a read-only media folder.
Generate waveforms and non-destructive edit markers instead of rewriting source files.
Implement silence trimming, loudness normalization to -16 LUFS, fades, and noise-gate presets.
Add chapter markers, intro and outro slots, and a simple two-track timeline.
Produce a transcript and draft title, description, chapters, and social excerpts.
Export MP3, WAV, transcript, chapters JSON, and a complete project manifest.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out real-time remote recording.
Deliberately leave out podcast hosting and directory analytics.
Deliberately leave out licensed stock music and voice cloning.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
